title: Sentinel is Cooking!
author: CellistAgitated7287
selftext:
Every time I missed a big move, the narrative had already been building for days.  
  
GME. NVDA's AI run. The COIN pump before the ETF approval. In hindsight, the chatter was loud. On Reddit, on X, in niche Discord servers. But I was reading earnings reports and watching price action  -  the same data everyone else had.  
  
That's the problem. Retail investors are trained to look at lagging indicators. Price already moved. Volume already spiked. The institutional players who got in early? They were watching sentiment shift in real time.  
  
Hedge funds have been running social sentiment models for years. They scrape forums, scan trending topics, track narrative momentum before it hits price. It's not a secret  -  it's just expensive infrastructure most individuals can't build.  
  
So I started tracking it manually. Scanning Reddit threads, tagging recurring tickers, noting when sentiment on a name shifted from skeptical to excited before any price movement confirmed it. It worked. It was also completely unsustainable.  
  
That frustration is what led me to build Sentinel  -  an AI-powered sentiment dashboard that does this automatically. It monitors social media in real time, generates sentiment scores (think Fear/Greed scale per ticker), surfaces trending topics tied to specific assets, and fires trade signals based on sentiment shift patterns.  
  
I'm not claiming it prints money. But it gives retail investors the same category of signal that institutional desks have been using for a decade.  
  
Curious whether anyone else has tried to incorporate social sentiment into their process  -  and what you actually found useful vs. noise. Check it out here: [https://sentinelmarkets.io/](https://sentinelmarkets.io/)

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: hindsight is doing most of the work there. GME chatter was loud, but so was chatter on fifty names that went nowhere that month, and nobody remembers those. the fizzles are the stat that matters, how often a shift fired and price just sat there.
